question: A 29-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 20 minutes after sustaining a gunshot wound to the abdomen. On arrival, he is awake and oriented to person, place, and time. He appears agitated. His pulse is 102/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 115/70 mm Hg. The pupils are equal and reactive to light. Abdominal examination shows an entrance wound in the right upper quadrant above the umbilicus. There is an exit wound on the right lower back next to the lumbar spine. Breath sounds are normal bilaterally. There is diffuse mild tenderness to palpation with no guarding or rebound. Cardiac examination shows no abnormalities. Intravenous fluid therapy is begun. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Gunshot wound to abdomen" -> "Potential internal bleeding" -> "Hemodynamic stability" -> "Immediate laparotomy" -> 85%
CHAIN: "Gunshot wound to abdomen" -> "Potential organ injury" -> "Stable vital signs" -> "CT scan of the abdomen" -> 70%
CHAIN: "Gunshot wound to abdomen" -> "Stable hemodynamics" -> "Potential for delayed complications" -> "Close observation" -> 60%
CHAIN: "Gunshot wound to abdomen" -> "Potential peritoneal penetration" -> "Need for rapid assessment" -> "Diagnostic peritoneal lavage" -> 65%
CHAIN: "Gunshot wound to abdomen" -> "Potential intra-abdominal injury" -> "Need for direct visualization" -> "Diagnostic laparoscopy" -> 50%
analysis: The patient has sustained a gunshot wound to the abdomen with an entrance wound in the right upper quadrant and an exit wound in the right lower back. Given the trajectory of the bullet, there is a high risk of intra-abdominal injury, potentially involving the liver, intestines, or other structures. Although the patient is hemodynamically stable at the moment, the presence of a gunshot wound with potential for significant internal injury necessitates surgical exploration. Immediate laparotomy is indicated in cases of penetrating abdominal trauma with potential for significant internal injury, even if the patient is currently stable, to prevent complications from undiagnosed injuries.
